one_line_positioning: Two structurally different threats surround the "big five" prompt-to-app builders: incumbent hosts (Hostinger, Wix, Google) that bundle the AI builder into an existing domain+email+hosting account so the paywall lands on infrastructure rather than tokens, and design/agent tools (Figma Make, Replit, AI Studio) that have solved the direct-manipulation editing loop the chat-only builders still haven't.
summary:
This sweep covers fourteen adjacent products, none of which is a direct Lovable/Bolt/v0/Base44 clone, and the interesting signal is that the category has split into three camps with very different answers to the same problems.

**Camp 1 — hosts who bolted an AI builder onto an existing account (Hostinger, Wix, Google).** Hostinger Horizons is the closest structural analogue to Remixer and the most instructive. It is not a standalone funnel at all: you reach it through hPanel → Websites → "Add website" → Hostinger Horizons, so the builder is a feature of a hosting account, not a product with its own front door. The consequence is that every plan is priced as *hosting with AI credits attached* rather than *AI with hosting attached*: Free (5 credits, 1 site), Explorer $6.99/mo (30 credits, 1 mailbox), Starter $13.99/mo (70 credits, 25 sites, free domain, 2 mailboxes), Hobbyist $39.99/mo (200 credits, 50 sites, free domain, 5 mailboxes, code editor). Mailboxes are a per-tier ladder — this is exactly the lever DreamHost has and Lovable/Bolt do not, and Hostinger is already pulling it. Wix does the same at scale: all four paid plans (Light $17, Core $29, Business $39, Business Elite $159, annual) include a free custom domain for year one, and Wix Harmony — launched January 2026 — is a hybrid "vibe coding meets drag and drop" editor with the Aria agent embedded in the visual editor rather than beside it. Google is a third variant: AI Studio Build mode ships apps to free `name.ai.studio` subdomains (July 10 2026) and free Cloud Run deploys with no credit card, funding the whole thing as Gemini API demand generation. Firebase Studio, its predecessor, was shut down 19 March 2026 — Google consolidated.

**Camp 2 — design/agent tools that solved direct manipulation.** Figma Make's July 30 2026 update is the single most valuable thing in this sweep. It added a right-hand properties panel with a full DOM tree, spacing/type/layout/opacity/z-index/radius controls bound to codebase tokens, and — critically — *every direct manipulation stages in the prompt box, credit-free, until you hit apply*. Only on apply does Make burn credits and cut a new version. That is a complete answer to the "chat edits cost money for a 4px nudge" complaint that plagues every credit-metered builder including Remixer. Alongside it sits "Annotate for agent": numbered blue callouts you drop on canvas plus intent-level language ("make this section feel calmer"). Replit reaches the same place from the other side: its Element Editor lets you change text, font size/weight, alignment, text and background colour, margin and padding as direct source edits that consume **no credits**, escalating to Agent only when scope exceeds that. Google AI Studio's "Design Variations" (mid-July 2026) is the cheapest trick in the category: one click produces five complete alternative design directions — layout, colour, typography — which you preview and apply, replacing the aesthetic re-prompting loop entirely. It's free.

**Camp 3 — agent-maximalists (Replit, Emergent, Anything).** Replit Agent 3 (Sept 2025) introduced in-pane browser self-testing: the agent opens a real browser and you watch its cursor click around inside the Agent pane, with up to 200 minutes of autonomous runtime and a "Max Autonomy (Beta)" toggle in the Agent Tools section of the input box. Agent 4 replaced the Design Mode tab with an infinite "Design Canvas", moved collaboration from fork-and-merge to one shared project with per-person chat threads and a Kanban board (Drafts / Active / Ready / Done), and lets you open a planning chat while the main build still runs. Emergent runs a named multi-agent crew and shows real-time build steps with self-taken verification screenshots.

**The domain/DNS finding matters most for us.** Replit — not a registrar, not a host in the DreamHost sense — has closed the gap Remixer still has open. Its release notes record "custom domain DNS setup automated" on 5 June 2026, implemented via **Entri**, a third-party service that signs into the user's registrar and writes the records on their behalf. Replit also sells domains in-app across .com/.ai with auto-DNS, "less than a minute from search to going live". Emergent, a pure AI startup, resells IONOS domains from a "Link Domain" button inside the Deployments panel, free for the first year, SSL auto-provisioned in under ten minutes. So the category has independently converged on exactly the capability DreamHost is structurally best placed to own but currently lacks (Domain Connect). Figma, by contrast, still makes users paste TXT + CNAME records manually and press "Refresh".

**Money.** Credit metering is universally the loudest complaint. Figma enforced Full-seat AI credit limits from 18 March 2026 (3,000/mo Professional, 3,500 Org, 4,250 Enterprise, no rollover) and the forum filled with users reporting 200,000→3,000 credit cliffs and $200+ overage months. Replit's effort-based billing produced "bill shock" threads and a Register story about surprise overruns at Agent 3 launch. Hostinger's 30-credit Explorer tier is widely called punishing, made worse by paywalling the code editor at $39.99 so cheap-tier users must spend a credit on every CSS tweak. Framer publishes an unusually honest per-action price list (~300 credits for a landing page, 150 responsive layout, 100 large edit, 50 small edit) with model multipliers. Emergent charges 50 credits/month as ongoing rent for an active deployment.

findings.title: Wix Harmony's landing page is a prompt box with a pre-flight 'Refine my prompt' button
findings.detail: wix.com/harmony hero reads "Where vibe coding meets drag and drop freedom". Centre is a large open text field with placeholder "Describe the website you want". Below it four quick-start tags — Fashion Store, Online Course, Wellness Services, Consulting Website — plus a "More Ideas" button. Two actions sit on the box: "Refine my prompt" (AI improves your brief BEFORE generating) and "Generate My Site". A persistent disclaimer reads "AI can make mistakes. Always double-check the results." The 'refine before you spend' step is a pattern none of the big five run at the landing-page level.

findings.title: Wix Harmony runs a conversational interview before generating, not a single prompt
findings.detail: Aria asks a short back-and-forth: what the site is about, what to call it, who it's for, and the desired tone (reviewers cite options phrased as warm and playful / clean and professional / bold and modern). Reviewers rate the interview highly but note the AI "asks the right questions but does not help you answer them" — users stall at the unique-selling-point question. First usable draft appears in 4–7 minutes; prompt-to-live-URL is quoted at roughly 5–7 minutes.

findings.title: Emergent puts the auth wall BEFORE the prompt box — the inverse of category norm
findings.detail: An Aug 5 2026 hands-on review reports the initial screen prioritises authentication over prompt entry, explicitly noting this differentiates it from competing vibe-coding tools. Sign-in offers email, Google, GitHub and — unusually for a dev tool — Facebook. During setup the product asks the user which OTHER vibe-coding tools they already use, i.e. it collects competitive intel as an onboarding question.

findings.title: Hostinger Horizons has no standalone funnel — it lives inside the hosting control panel
findings.detail: Official tutorial: entry is hPanel → Websites → "Add website" → select "Hostinger Horizons", enter your initial prompt, then "choose a domain or use a temporary one" — domain choice happens BEFORE the build, not after. A 7-day free trial requires no payment info; the free plan gives 5 AI credits and 1 website. This is the structural mirror of Remixer's position and the domain decision is pulled forward into onboarding.

findings.title: Replit's prompt box front-loads artifact type via a carousel of ten options
findings.detail: Docs show the agent input as a textarea plus a carousel of output types: Web, Mobile, Slides, Animation, Design, Data Visualization, Automation, 3D Game, Document, Spreadsheet. Alongside sit a "Plan" mode toggle, a microphone, and an arrow start button. Agent 4 later relaxed this — you no longer pre-select the artifact type and can "build slides, a website, a web app, or even a mobile app" inside one project.

findings.title: Replit exposes cost/quality as an explicit user-facing mode switch: Lite / Economy / Power + Turbo
findings.detail: Agent modes are switchable in-product: Lite (quick edits), Economy (cost-optimised), Power (higher-performance models). Docs verbatim: "In Advanced settings, you can also turn on Turbo for up to 2.5x faster builds at higher cost (Pro and Enterprise)." Making the speed/cost trade explicit rather than hidden is a credible answer to credit-anxiety.

findings.title: Figma Make plan mode produces an editable plan.md before any code is written
findings.detail: Activate via the mode dropdown in the prompt box or by typing "/plan". Make generates a structured plan in real time; it appears in chat AND creates a plan markdown file that opens automatically. You edit plan.md directly or keep chatting to revise — "There's no limit to how many times you can refine before approving" — then click a "Build" button in the chat. Constraints: paid plans only, default model or Claude Opus 4.7 only (not Gemini), and it consumes MORE credits than standard build mode.

findings.title: Google AI Studio ships an 'I'm Feeling Lucky' button and typed capability chips in the prompt box
findings.detail: Build mode's input box includes an "I'm Feeling Lucky" button that generates a creative project prompt for users with no idea, plus "AI Chips" for attaching specific capabilities to the prompt — the docs name image generation and Google Maps data as examples. Capability chips turn 'what can this thing even do' from a docs problem into an inline affordance.

findings.title: Replit Agent 3 shows a live browser inside the Agent pane with the agent's own cursor moving
findings.detail: App Testing is on by default with a toggle in the "Agent Tools section of the input box". When active, the agent periodically tests the app in a real browser and the UI displays "a browser preview within the Agent pane, showing the Agent's cursor as it clicks around." Replit claims this is 3x faster and 10x more cost-effective than Computer Use models. Watching the agent QA its own work is the most legible progress signal in the category — far better than a spinner or a streaming file tree.

findings.title: Hostinger Horizons plays a completion SOUND when publish finishes, plus a loading percentage
findings.detail: Official support doc: the editor displays a loading percentage indicator during publish; on completion "a completion sound confirms the site is live" and a dropdown appears with two actions — "Copy URL" and "Go to Analytics". Audio confirmation on a long async action is rare in this category and cheap to copy.

findings.title: Emergent narrates granular build steps and self-verifies with screenshots during a ~10-minute first build
findings.detail: Hands-on (Aug 2026): during the roughly 10-minute initial build the pane shows real-time steps including "breaking down prompt details, paths, image generation, package installations". The agent takes screenshots to verify its own output, self-diagnoses issues, fixes UI navigation problems, and asks clarifying questions mid-build when the prompt is under-specified — i.e. the clarification loop happens DURING generation rather than before it.

findings.title: Wix Harmony blocks multitasking mid-generation with a 'Don't leave this tab' modal
findings.detail: A reviewer documents a modal warning "Don't leave this tab" appearing mid-generation, explaining that leaving the browser tab would interrupt the build. Reviewers flag this as a genuine constraint for users who tab-switch constantly. Notable as an anti-pattern: it converts a 5-minute wait into 5 minutes of enforced attention.

findings.title: Hostinger Horizons puts the AI chat on the RIGHT and the site-management sidebar on the LEFT
findings.detail: Official tutorial describes three zones: a left sidebar behind a "≡" icon (contains "Monthly AI credits" with a usage graph, upgrade and top-up links, dashboard link, and buttons for "Create new website", "Duplicate this website", "Account sharing"); a centre live preview; and a right chat panel holding conversation history. Top nav has "Ask AI" and "Publish". This is the mirror image of Remixer's left-chat/right-rail layout — worth noting that the other hosting-company builder chose the opposite handedness.

findings.title: Horizons' chat panel is drag-resizable with persisted width, drag-to-hide, and double-click reset
findings.detail: Support docs: on desktop you resize the chat panel by dragging its edge and "your preferred width is saved". Drag the handle fully to one side to hide the panel entirely; double-click the handle to reset to default width. Three interactions on one drag handle — a small, high-quality detail that respects that some sessions are chat-heavy and some are preview-heavy.

findings.title: Horizons' centre canvas has a four-way mode toggle: Preview / Edit content / Code / Data
findings.detail: The preview area carries refresh and home icon buttons, a device toggle for mobile responsiveness, a fullscreen option, and an editor-mode toggle across Preview, Edit content, Code, and Data. Exposing the DATA layer as a peer of code and preview — a first-class tab rather than a buried tool — is unusual and directly relevant to Remixer's database feature.

findings.title: Replit swaps the preview pane for an admin dashboard when the artifact isn't a website
findings.detail: For Agents & Automations, "on one side of the workspace you'll see the Agent pane, and on the other side, instead of a preview you'll see an admin dashboard where you can test your chatbot or workflow automation." The shell keeps its two-pane rhythm but changes what the right pane means per artifact type — a cleaner solution than forcing everything into a browser preview.

findings.title: Replit consolidated infrastructure into one pinned Tools pane on 31 July 2026
findings.detail: Release note verbatim: "The new pinned Tools pane brings Database, Auth, Domains, Secrets, and more together in a single place." Prior to this these were scattered. Directly comparable to Remixer's right icon rail — Replit's read is that infra tools want to be one pinned surface, not a rail of unrelated icons.

findings.title: Replit Agent 4 replaced fork-and-merge collaboration with one shared project + a Kanban board
findings.detail: Agent 4 changes: the standalone Design Mode tab becomes a "Design Canvas" described as "an infinite canvas that sits at the center of the design workflow" working across all artifact types; collaboration drops forking/merging so "everyone works in the same project" with individual chat threads and "a shared Kanban board organized into four columns: Drafts, Active, Ready, and Done"; and planning is now parallel — you can "open a new chat to plan with the Agent while your main build is still running". Agent-assisted conflict resolution removes manual merging.

findings.title: 'Max Autonomy (Beta)' and a 200-minute runtime are surfaced as a user-controllable dial
findings.detail: Agent 3 runs autonomously for up to 200 minutes (10x Agent 2's ~20 min). "Max Autonomy (Beta)" lets the Agent run longer without user input, with self-supervision monitoring its own progress. Autonomy-as-a-slider rather than a fixed product behaviour is a pattern the chat-only builders don't offer.

findings.title: Softr's AI Co-Builder interviews on BUSINESS logic, then narrates every schema decision as it builds
findings.detail: Before generating, the Co-Builder asks clarifying questions about business context rather than technical detail: what asset types clients will review, how approval flows should work, who should see what. During the build, "On the right, the database takes shape in real time... On the left, Softr narrates every decision it makes. Why it created certain fields, how it linked tables, what logic it applied." Reviewers note you then refine visually with drag-and-drop "so you are never trapped in a re-prompting loop". Time to something real: under 20 minutes.

findings.title: Figma made agent chats visible to teammates by default (Config 2026)
findings.detail: Config 2026 update: "Agent chats are also now visible to your teammates by default, so you can see what directions others are exploring and build on their thinking." Turning the prompt log into a shared artifact rather than a private session is a genuinely novel collaboration primitive — the prompt history becomes team knowledge.

findings.title: Figma Make stages direct visual edits in the prompt box, credit-free, until you apply them
findings.detail: July 30 2026: a properties panel on the RIGHT of the Make editor with a full DOM tree (layers view for code) exposes spacing, padding, typography (line height, letter spacing, weights), layout, opacity, z-index, borders, corner radius, and colour/type tokens pulled from your codebase. You can "select every instance of an element at once to update them together". Critically, direct manipulations "stage every edit in the prompt box so you can review each change before you commit to it, or discard anything that doesn't look right" — edits accumulate "staged and credit-free, until you apply them". Only on apply does Make burn credits and cut a new file version. This is the strongest single pattern in the whole sweep.

findings.title: Figma Make 'Annotate for agent' drops numbered blue callouts on canvas for intent-level requests
findings.detail: Selecting "Annotate for agent" in the top-right toolbar (which now carries both "Edit" and "Annotate for agent") activates annotation mode: numbered blue callouts appear on-canvas marking specific elements, and you describe the change contextually — Figma's own examples are "when you hover over this thumbnail, have it zoom in slightly" and "make this section feel calmer". The point is annotations carry things "easier to say than to click" — vague aesthetic intent bound to a precise target.

findings.title: Replit's Element Editor makes a defined set of edits FREE by writing source directly, no agent involved
findings.detail: Verbatim: "Click any element in your app's preview to start editing. Directly edit text if it's a string in your source code, right from the app preview!" Credit-free direct edits cover text content, font size, font weight, text alignment, text colour, background colour, margin and padding, with an eyedropper-capable colour picker accepting names and hex. Changes preview live. For anything larger it "seamlessly sends targeted metadata to Agent". A published free/paid boundary drawn at 'does this need the model' rather than 'is this an edit'.

findings.title: Google AI Studio 'Design Variations': one click generates five complete alternative design directions
findings.detail: Shipped mid-July 2026, free. You describe or open a page and click once; AI Studio produces five different design versions with distinct layouts, colour approaches and typographic choices. You preview and compare the proposals, then apply the chosen one to the app in Build with one action "rather than re-prompting from scratch". Gemini 3.5 Flash (default since May 2026) is credited as the speed enabler. This replaces the aesthetic re-prompting loop — the single most credit-wasteful behaviour in every metered builder — with a mouse click.

findings.title: Google AI Studio annotation mode lets you literally draw on the running app in the preview window
findings.detail: I/O 2026: a new tool lets developers "annotate right in the preview window. Draw on your app, tweak components and generate new visuals." Coverage describes highlighting any section of a live app and typing the change — working for layout adjustments, copy changes, colour updates and structural edits. Paired with Nano Banana, the Build agent "can automatically generate custom images on the fly", so asset generation is inline rather than a separate tool.

findings.title: Hostinger's select-and-edit scopes the NEXT prompt rather than performing an edit
findings.detail: The "Select and edit" tool lets you "click a specific element on your website and apply changes only to that section in your next prompt". Separately, "Edit Content" mode lets you click directly on any static text or image in the preview and edit it immediately without the AI. Two distinct mechanisms — one scopes the model, one bypasses it — where most builders conflate them.

findings.title: Hostinger's Undo and Restore are DESTRUCTIVE and refund nothing — with explicit warning copy
findings.detail: Undo is a curved-arrow icon below the most recent chat message; using it means "your last message and the Horizon's corresponding response are permanently deleted". Restore sits under any earlier message and confirms with "All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted." Docs state plainly: "Undoing or restoring a version does not cost additional credits and does not reinstate credits spent on the reverted messages." Honest, but a linear destructive history rather than branchable checkpoints.

findings.title: Figma Make has NO file-level version history — versions are builds living inside the chat
findings.detail: Figma's own answer: there is no additional file-level version history in a Make file; in a Make file "versions" refer to the different builds of the project. You recover earlier work by reviewing the versions shared in the AI chat and clicking a "Restore this version" icon next to the file you want to revert. A live feature request thread exists asking for real version history. For a company whose core product's version history is a flagship feature, this is a conspicuous gap.

findings.title: Hostinger paywalls the code editor two tiers up, forcing every CSS tweak through paid credits
findings.detail: The code editor and file-structure view appear only on Hobbyist ($39.99/mo) and above. On Explorer ($6.99) and Starter ($13.99) "you can't touch the generated code. Every change goes through the AI, which means every change costs a credit." Reviewers explicitly recommend Hobbyist on the grounds that "the code editor access changes the economics: you stop burning credits on small CSS tweaks". A paywall that makes the cheap tiers structurally more expensive to use.

findings.title: Figma Make lets you switch device frames while editing, not only in a preview mode
findings.detail: July 30 2026: device frame previews were added so you "see designs across screen sizes by switching device frames as they edit, so the design holds up everywhere". Combined with the properties panel this means responsive checking happens inside the editing loop rather than as a separate verification step.

findings.title: Emergent's browser previews expire after 30 minutes
findings.detail: Hands-on review flags browser-based previews expiring after 30 minutes as "a significant constraint for extended work sessions". Mobile apps preview only through Expo Go rather than the browser. An ephemeral-preview model that punishes exactly the long iterative sessions the product is sold on.

findings.title: Replit, Emergent and Anything all converge on the same mobile-preview UX: QR code + Expo Go
findings.detail: Replit runs a fully managed React Native + Expo pipeline that is invisible to the user; the console displays a QR code linking Expo Go to the project — scan it and the app loads on your phone, save and reload to see updates. Emergent does the same. Deployment options at Emergent are permanent Expo Go access, iOS IPA download, and Android APK/AAB download. The scan-to-preview handoff has become the category-standard bridge from browser builder to physical device.

findings.title: Figma Make's publish modal contains a typography warning nobody else has
findings.detail: "Publish" sits in the upper-right. The modal fields are Title (described as how it appears "in browser tabs, search engine results, and social media"), URL, Status ("Not published" / "Published"), a Typography alert about missing web fonts (WOFF/WOFF2), and "Who can view" on Org/Enterprise. Auto-generated URLs take the format three-random-words.figma.site. After first publish the primary button becomes "Update". Unpublish lives under "Make settings" — which also holds meta description, language, Google Analytics ID, search-engine exclusion, favicon, access management, social sharing image, and custom head/body code. Catching a font that will render wrong in production, inside the publish modal, is a craft detail worth stealing.

findings.title: Figma Make defaults published sites to NOT indexed by search engines
findings.detail: Verbatim from the FAQ: "By default, your published functional prototype or web app won't be indexed by search engines." Visibility tiers are Public (default), Internal-only (Org/Enterprise, logged-in org members only), and optional password protection. Hosting runs on AWS with Cloudflare for domain/routing. A prototype-first default that reads as considerate rather than restrictive — the opposite bet from site builders where SEO is the point.

findings.title: Replit prices deployment separately from the AI subscription, and democratised private publishing
findings.detail: Deployment types are Autoscale ("Automatically adjusts resources based on your app's usage"), Static ("an affordable way to host websites that don't change based on user input"), Reserved VM, and Scheduled. Scheduled and autoscale start at $1/month; reserved VM starts at $20/month, on top of the plan. Access controls are described as "Control who can see your app with a single click", and a 8 May 2026 release note records private publishing being extended from Pro/Enterprise down to Core and Starter. Free Starter includes "private/password-protected deployments".

findings.title: Replit automated external-registrar DNS using Entri — closing exactly the gap Remixer still has
findings.detail: Replit's docs state it "offers automated DNS configuration using Entri, a third-party service that can sign into your registrar and write records on your behalf, bypassing manual entry." A 5 June 2026 release note records "Custom domain DNS setup automated; users no longer need manual record configuration." This is the direct answer to DreamHost's verified Aug 2026 Domain Connect gap — a non-registrar solved it by buying the capability, and it is available off the shelf.

findings.title: Replit sells domains in-app and lands them in under a minute; the verification TXT must live forever
findings.detail: Under the Publishing tool's Domains tab you choose "Buy a new domain" (search across .com, .ai and more, purchase in-app, "Your domain will automatically be configured to point to your Replit app") or "Connect your own domain". Marketing claim: "The entire process takes less than a minute from search to going live." A 10 July 2026 release note records domain purchasing integrated without an external registrar account. Manual connection needs an A record plus a TXT record "replit-verify=..." which must remain in DNS permanently — removing it breaks certificate renewal and eventually takes the domain down. Status flips to "Verified".

findings.title: Emergent — a pure AI startup, not a host — resells IONOS domains free for year one, in-flow
findings.detail: From the Deployments panel's Custom Domain section you click "Link Domain", search a name with real-time availability checked against IONOS, and buy it without leaving Emergent. "The domain registration through IONOS is free for the first year", then standard IONOS renewal pricing. Emergent configures DNS automatically, SSL certificates "are provisioned" on connection, and the whole thing "typically takes less than 10 minutes, most of which is DNS propagation time". For an existing domain, Emergent supplies an A record with TTL 300; verification takes 5–15 minutes. A startup has manufactured registrar economics that DreamHost owns natively.

findings.title: Figma still makes users copy TXT + CNAME by hand — the weakest domain flow in the sweep
findings.detail: Settings → Domains under Site → "Add connected domain" → enter domain → for apex or www choose redirect preference via a toggle → sign into your registrar → "Add the TXT and CNAME record provided by Figma to your DNS settings" → return to Figma and click "Refresh". SSL is auto-provisioned after verification; the process "typically takes up to 15 minutes, but can sometimes require additional time", with an error icon if records can't be verified. Professional plans cap at 10 custom domains shared between Make and Sites; Org/Enterprise unlimited.

findings.title: Google AI Studio gives every published app a free branded subdomain, first-come-first-served
findings.detail: Shipped 10 July 2026: deployed apps claim free custom subdomains in the form yourapp.ai.studio. You enter the subdomain you want or accept Google's suggestion before deploying. Names are unique platform-wide and assigned first-come, first-served. Building, publishing and getting the link all cost nothing, and "your code and chat history stay private". Reporting frames this as removing Cloud Run as a prerequisite for shipping. Compare Remixer's *.remixer.app staging subdomain — same mechanic, but Google positions it as the permanent public address rather than staging.

findings.title: Hostinger sells mailboxes as an explicit per-tier ladder inside the AI builder's pricing table
findings.detail: Mailboxes per website by tier: Free none, Explorer 1, Starter 2, Hobbyist 5. Free domain from Starter upward. This is the clearest evidence in the sweep that a host is already monetising email through the AI-builder funnel — precisely the lever DreamHost holds and Lovable/Bolt/v0/Base44 structurally cannot pull.

findings.title: Hostinger's own docs warn that changing a Horizons project's domain destroys the email plan
findings.detail: Domain management doc carries an explicit warning that changing the domain in hPanel's Websites list "resets your email plan and deletes all associated email data" and advises backing up first; subdomains also require manual updates. Domain redirection is not built into Horizons at all — you leave for hPanel → Domains → "Forward Domain", choose HTTP/HTTPS and 302 vs permanent, then "Create". The bundled-stack advantage is real but the seams between builder and control panel are visible and dangerous.

findings.title: Wix monetises the domain on a year-one-free / renew-at-retail model across every paid tier
findings.detail: All four paid Wix plans (Light $17, Core $29, Business $39, Business Elite $159 per month on annual billing; $24/$36/$46/$172 monthly) include a free custom domain for the first year, with renewal at roughly $17.35/year afterwards. Email is not bundled the way Hostinger bundles mailboxes — it is sold separately. Wix's site-building AI (Harmony, Aria) is therefore funded by hosting+domain subscription rather than metered credits.

findings.title: Framer publishes an unusually transparent per-action credit price list, including model multipliers
findings.detail: Reported credit costs: a full landing page ~300 credits, a responsive layout 150, a large edit 100, a small edit 50. Allowances: Free 500 credits per DAY (resets daily, no rollover — roughly two landing pages), Basic 1,000/month, Pro 3,000/month, both with add-anytime top-ups. Model multipliers apply: Sonnet 4.6 at 0.9x base cost, Opus 4.8 at 1.8x. External agents (e.g. Claude Code via MCP) consume no Framer credits. Publishing a Framer subdomain site with SSL is free on the free plan; a custom domain requires Basic or higher.

findings.title: Figma enforced hard AI credit caps on 18 March 2026 and the forum revolted
findings.detail: Full-seat monthly allowances: 3,000 on Professional (≈50–70 Make prompts), 3,500 on Organization, 4,250 on Enterprise. Starter and View seats capped at 500/month PLUS a 150/day limit. Credits reset monthly with no rollover. Before 18 March 2026 Full-seat limits were not enforced; after that date a seat that hits its cap loses AI features until reset even if team-level credits remain. From 11 March 2026 teams can buy a shared AI credits subscription; pay-as-you-go with a spending limit arrived in Q2 2026. Forum posts report a user's usage collapsing from ~200,000 credits/month to 3,000 (a 98.5% reduction) and a $200+ overage month on a single project.

findings.title: Emergent charges recurring credit RENT for keeping an app deployed
findings.detail: Plans: Free $0/10 credits, Standard $20/mo ($17 annual) with 100 credits, Pro $200/mo ($167 annual) with 750 credits, Team $300/mo with 1,250 shared credits. Top-ups $10 for 50 credits, never expire. Critically, an active deployment costs 50 credits per month on an ongoing basis — so a shipped app consumes half a Standard plan's monthly allowance just by existing. Private project hosting starts at Standard.

findings.title: Replit's free Starter tier lets you publish one project — the paywall lands on scale, not on shipping
findings.detail: Starter (free): free daily Agent credits, built-in database, slides/videos/animations, "publish up to 1 project", and private/password-protected deployments. Core $20/mo billed annually ($25 monthly) with $25 monthly credits, 5 collaborators, 2 parallel agents, branding-badge removal. Pro $95/mo annually ($100 monthly) with $100 credits, 15 collaborators, 50 viewers, 10 parallel agents, 28-day database rollbacks. "Effort-Based Pricing (pay-as-you-go)" is listed as a FAQ topic without definition on the pricing page itself — the opacity is deliberate and is the root of the bill-shock complaints.

findings.title: Hostinger states plainly that credit cost scales with generation complexity
findings.detail: Verbatim from the pricing page: "AI credits are used when you create or edit websites by chatting with AI. Credit usage depends on the complexity of each generation." Ladder: Free $0/5 credits/1 site/no mailbox/no domain; Explorer $6.99 (reg. $9.99) / 30 credits / 1 site / 1 mailbox; Starter $13.99 (reg. $19.99) / 70 credits / 25 sites / 2 mailboxes / free domain; Hobbyist $39.99 (reg. $55.99) / 200 credits / 50 sites / 5 mailboxes / free domain / code editor. A Hustler tier at $59.99–$79.99 with 400 credits is cited by reviewers. Renewal equals promo price on the tiers listed.

findings.title: Replit ships a real native mobile app with voice building and remote build monitoring
findings.detail: Free iOS and Android app: "Create, share, and publish web apps all from the palm of your hand." Projects sync between desktop and mobile, Agent is available on mobile, and you can publish from the phone. Agent 3 marketing adds that you can "track your project's progress, in real time, on your home page on the web or live monitoring on your phone". A 24 July 2026 release note records a mobile refresh with improved navigation and voice building — describing projects aloud. Replit is explicit that it "is not an app store and does not distribute apps directly to mobile devices"; native iOS submission requires the web product.

findings.title: Google opened pre-registration for an AI Studio mobile app at I/O 2026
findings.detail: Announced as letting builders "iterate on code and preview builds directly from your pocket" and start projects on the go. Same release added native Android app generation inside AI Studio — select "Build an Android app", get Kotlin with Jetpack Compose, and use "an Android Emulator running in the browser" plus ADB support for installing to a device. Figma Make is also accessible through the Figma mobile app.

findings.title: Google AI Studio's app gallery is a remixable browse-preview-fork surface, not a static template list
findings.detail: Docs describe a visual gallery where developers can "browse what's possible with Gemini, preview applications instantly, and remix them." Replit's Design product takes a related approach with "Templates and inspiration you can add at any moment", powered by Mobbin, injectable mid-project rather than only at start. Both treat inspiration as an in-session escape hatch from a stuck build, not a pre-generation choice.

findings.title: Claude Artifacts inverts hosting economics: the VIEWER's plan pays for the app's AI usage
findings.detail: Anthropic's model: share an AI-powered artifact by link; viewers "authenticate with their existing Claude account", "Their API usage counts against their subscription, not yours", "You pay nothing for their usage", and no one manages API keys. Creators bear zero infrastructure cost. Artifacts are forkable and customisable by viewers. Later coverage reports persistent storage (up to 20MB per artifact), direct API calls, MCP integrations and live-refreshing artifacts. Original announcement is dated 25 July 2025, so treat later capability claims as less firm.

findings.title: Replit Connectors: 450+ services, MCP-powered, authenticate once and reuse across every project
findings.detail: The Connectors platform launched with 24 pre-built MCP-powered integrations (Stripe, Figma, Zendesk, Salesforce, ClickUp cited) where users authenticate once per service and reuse that connection across multiple projects. A 26 June 2026 release note records the catalogue expanding to 450+ services in a redesigned browsable interface with category filters. Agent 3 additionally builds agents and automations for Slack, Telegram and timed triggers, with connectors for Notion, Linear, Dropbox and Sharepoint.

findings.title: Google AI Studio injects the API key server-side and gives two free Cloud deploys with no card
findings.detail: Docs: AI Studio configures GEMINI_API_KEY as a server-side secret — "API keys are injected into the server-side runtime and are never included in client-side code" — and the deployed app uses your key for all users' Gemini API calls. I/O 2026: newcomers can "deploy their first two apps to Google Cloud at no cost, no credit card required." A no-card trial framed per-artifact rather than per-time-window, which is a different shape from Remixer's 30-day model.

findings.title: Hostinger routes users to analytics from the publish success dropdown itself
findings.detail: After a successful publish the dropdown offers exactly two actions: "Copy URL" and "Go to Analytics". Post-launch measurement is offered at the single moment the user cares most, rather than being buried in a dashboard they must remember to revisit. Republishing an already-live site surfaces a "Publish changes" option in the same dropdown.

findings.title: Time-to-first-render across the sweep clusters at 4–10 minutes, materially slower than Remixer's 2–3
findings.detail: Wix Harmony: first usable version at 4–7 minutes, prompt-to-live-URL 5–7 minutes, with reviewers noting "slower initial generation" than pure AI builders as the cost of the hybrid editor. Hostinger Horizons: initial app generation ~5 minutes in a Dec 2025 hands-on. Emergent: ~10 minutes for the first build, with simple apps generated and deployed in under 10 minutes and complex builds usually under 30. Softr AI Co-Builder: "something real in front of you in under 20 minutes". Framer Wireframer is the outlier at under 60 seconds for a multi-page responsive wireframe.

findings.title: Google killed Firebase Studio on 19 March 2026 and consolidated everything into AI Studio
findings.detail: Firebase Studio (formerly Project IDX) shut down 19 March 2026 with Cloud IDE and AI code generation discontinued; existing projects remain accessible until March 2027 for migration. Before shutdown it was free to start with 3 workspaces (up to 30 via the Google Developer Program). Anyone benchmarking against Firebase Studio's App Prototyping agent should retarget to AI Studio Build mode. Treat the exact shutdown date as medium confidence — it comes from secondary coverage, not a Google page I could fetch.

findings.title: Wix runs THREE parallel AI builders — Harmony, Vibe and the acquired Base44
findings.detail: Wix Harmony launched January 2026 as the hybrid vibe-coding-plus-drag-and-drop editor. Wix is separately testing "Wix Vibe". Base44 was acquired in June 2025 for a reported $80M solo-founder exit, with Wix guiding to $50M ARR by year-end 2025. Wix returned to the Super Bowl in January 2026 to market this. The portfolio approach — one hybrid editor for SMBs, one code-first product, one acquired startup brand — is a hedge no other player in the sweep is running.

findings.title: Hostinger anchors its builder on a purple Publish button, top-right, matching Hostinger brand not a dark AI aesthetic
findings.detail: Walkthroughs describe clicking "the purple Publish button in the top right of the screen". Horizons deliberately reads as a Hostinger control-panel surface (hPanel chrome, hamburger sidebar, credits meter with usage graph) rather than adopting the dark-mode IDE aesthetic that Lovable, Bolt, v0 and Remixer share. The design bet is continuity with the hosting account, not membership of the AI-builder category.

findings.title: Figma Make and Framer both keep the AI inside an established design-tool visual language rather than inventing an AI chrome
findings.detail: Framer's editor "feels like Figma, with layers, frames, and auto-layout working as expected, and breakpoints being visual", with Wireframer and Workshop layered in as prompt surfaces inside that canvas. Figma Make added a properties panel that mirrors Figma Design's right rail, including a DOM tree presented as "layers view for code". Both products make the AI feel expensive by refusing to give it its own aesthetic — it inherits the credibility of the design tool around it. Specific typefaces, hex tokens, radii and easing values could not be verified without logging in; treat any such claim as unsourced.

findings.title: Framer Wireframer supplies a page-type button group under the prompt box to scaffold the brief
findings.detail: The Wireframer interface is described as two parts: a text input box for natural-language instructions, and a "Page Type Prompt Button Group" beneath it that inserts preset page-construction template commands. Reviewers report a prompt like "client portal for home services with login, request form, and dashboard" yielding a multi-page mobile-responsive wireframe with real copy in under 60 seconds. Injecting structured page-type tokens into an otherwise free-text prompt is a cheap accuracy win.

findings.title: Hostinger's docs teach an anti-pattern explicitly: restore immediately rather than fight an error loop
findings.detail: Guidance after a failed generation is to refine prompts, use manual edits for static elements, and "immediately restore rather than sending multiple fix attempts to avoid error loops". Docs also advise keeping prompts to no more than five actions per message for accuracy. Horizons additionally asks clarifying questions with CLICKABLE answer options alongside a free-text fallback — a structured-choice recovery affordance rather than pure open chat.

findings.title: Softr and Hostinger both surface the DATABASE as a first-class visible artifact during generation
findings.detail: Softr builds the schema visibly on the right while narrating field and relationship decisions on the left, producing database, UI, authentication, permissions, workflow automation and third-party integrations from the business interview. Hostinger exposes "Data" as a peer tab alongside Preview, Edit content and Code in the centre canvas. Contrast with most chat builders where the database is invisible until something breaks — making schema legible during generation is a trust mechanism, not just a feature.

findings.title: Figma Make ships a guidelines.md file in its code editor as the design-system contract
findings.detail: FAQ confirms a code editor for Full seats and drafts-only users, that you can "add your own code" and iterate conversationally, and that a guidelines.md file is available in the code editor for customisation. Separately, "Make kits" sync npm packages, library styles and guidelines into Make so generated interfaces follow predefined components, spacing, hierarchy and interaction patterns. The "Import from Figma" button was renamed "Attach a design" to reflect that you can paste Figma frames or drag-drop images directly.

standout_ux.name: Staged, credit-free visual edits (Figma Make)
standout_ux.what_it_is: A right-hand properties panel with a DOM tree lets you nudge spacing, type, colour, radius, opacity and z-index directly. Every manipulation STAGES in the prompt box, costs nothing, and can be reviewed or discarded. Only when you hit apply does Make spend credits and cut a new version.
standout_ux.why_it_works: It severs the link between 'I want to move this 4px' and 'that costs money', which is the single biggest source of resentment in every metered builder. It also converts the prompt box from a command line into a review queue — the user sees a batch of pending changes before committing, so the credit spend feels deliberate rather than extracted. Directly applicable to Remixer, where chat edits burn credits.

standout_ux.name: Free direct source edits with automatic escalation (Replit Element Editor)
standout_ux.what_it_is: Click any element in the preview. Text content, font size and weight, alignment, text and background colour, margin and padding are written straight to source with no agent call and no credits. Anything beyond that scope "seamlessly sends targeted metadata to Agent".
standout_ux.why_it_works: It draws the paid boundary at 'does this need the model' rather than 'is this an edit', which is defensible and easy to explain. The escalation is invisible — the user never has to decide which tool to reach for. A published, principled free tier inside a metered product buys enormous goodwill.

standout_ux.name: Design Variations — five directions from one click (Google AI Studio)
standout_ux.what_it_is: One button generates five complete alternative designs of the current page with different layouts, colour approaches and typography. You preview, compare, and apply one — no re-prompting, no aesthetic vocabulary required. Free, shipped mid-July 2026.
standout_ux.why_it_works: Aesthetic iteration is the most credit-wasteful and most frustrating loop in prompt-to-app: users don't have the language for what they want, so they spend six prompts circling it. Replacing that with parallel visual choice is both cheaper for the vendor and dramatically more satisfying. Nobody in the big five does this.

standout_ux.name: Entri-powered automatic DNS on external domains (Replit)
standout_ux.what_it_is: Rather than showing DNS records to copy, Replit uses Entri to sign into the user's registrar and write the A and TXT records on their behalf. A June 2026 release note simply says custom domain DNS setup is automated.
standout_ux.why_it_works: It is the exact capability DreamHost is missing (no Domain Connect as of Aug 2026) and it is buyable off the shelf. Replit — with none of DreamHost's registrar advantage — has already removed the worst step in going live. If we ship in-flow domain connection for DreamHost-held domains but still hand external users a table of records, Replit's flow will feel better than ours on the one journey we should own outright.

standout_ux.name: In-flow domain purchase with a free first year (Emergent, via IONOS)
standout_ux.what_it_is: A "Link Domain" button inside the Deployments panel searches live IONOS availability, buys the domain in-app free for year one, auto-configures DNS and provisions SSL in under ten minutes.
standout_ux.why_it_works: A pure AI startup manufactured registrar economics by reselling someone else's. It proves the in-flow buy-a-domain moment converts, and it sets the price expectation (free first year) that DreamHost can meet natively with better margin. This is the clearest evidence that our structural advantage has a short shelf life if we don't ship it.

standout_ux.name: The agent QA-ing itself in a visible browser (Replit Agent 3)
standout_ux.what_it_is: App Testing, toggled from the Agent Tools section of the input box, opens a real browser inside the Agent pane and you watch the agent's own cursor click through the app it just built, finding and fixing its own bugs.
standout_ux.why_it_works: It is the most legible generation state anyone has shipped. A build log says 'trust me'; a cursor clicking your own buttons says 'I checked'. It converts dead waiting time into something a non-technical user finds genuinely reassuring and even entertaining, and it pre-empts the 'it generated but it's broken' first impression.

standout_ux.name: Business-logic interview plus decision narration (Softr AI Co-Builder)
standout_ux.what_it_is: Before generating, it asks about business context, not technology: what asset types clients review, how approvals should flow, who sees what. During the build the database assembles visibly on the right while the left pane narrates each choice — why a field exists, how tables were linked, what logic was applied.
standout_ux.why_it_works: Two things at once: the questions are answerable by the actual buyer (a small-business owner can answer 'who approves this', not 'do you want a join table'), and the narration makes the invisible backend legible, which is exactly where AI builders lose non-technical trust. Highly relevant to Remixer's database, accounts and forms→DB features.

standout_ux.name: Annotate-for-agent numbered callouts (Figma Make)
standout_ux.what_it_is: Toolbar toggle drops numbered blue callouts on the canvas; you pin vague intent to a precise target — Figma's own examples are "make this section feel calmer" and "when you hover over this thumbnail, have it zoom in slightly".
standout_ux.why_it_works: It solves the deixis problem — users say 'this bit' and gesture at their screen. Click-to-select scopes WHERE but forces the user to also articulate WHAT precisely; annotations let the where be precise and the what be loose, which matches how people actually talk about design.

standout_ux.name: A resize handle that does three things (Hostinger Horizons)
standout_ux.what_it_is: Drag the chat panel edge to resize and the width persists across sessions; drag fully to one side to hide the panel; double-click to reset to default.
standout_ux.why_it_works: Cheap, and it acknowledges that a session is either chat-heavy or preview-heavy and the user knows which. Persistence is the part most builders skip. Remixer's ~408px chat panel is currently fixed.

standout_ux.name: Publish-modal font warning and a completion sound (Figma Make / Hostinger)
standout_ux.what_it_is: Figma's publish modal contains a Typography alert flagging missing WOFF/WOFF2 web fonts before you go live. Hostinger plays an audible completion sound on successful publish and immediately offers "Copy URL" and "Go to Analytics".
standout_ux.why_it_works: Both treat publish as a moment deserving craft rather than a state change. Catching the one thing that reliably renders wrong in production, at the exact instant it can still be fixed, is the kind of detail that makes an interface feel expensive. And a sound plus two next-actions turns a terminal moment into a beginning.

weaknesses.issue: Credit metering produces bill shock and destroys workflows when limits are enforced retroactively
weaknesses.evidence: Figma forum threads after the 18 March 2026 enforcement date report a user's normal usage dropping from ~200,000 credits/month to 3,000 (98.5% reduction), one user consuming ~269,000 credits in two weeks against a top credit package of ~15,000 for about $350, a thread titled about paying $200+ after two months inside base credits, and a thread arguing extra credits are 5.6x more expensive than simply adding a secondary seat. Thread titles include "Figma Make Ai Credit Limits Not Feasible" and "Complaints about AI credit usage".

weaknesses.issue: Replit's effort-based billing is unpredictable and users cannot forecast cost
weaknesses.evidence: The Register (18 Sept 2025) reported Agent 3 pricing infuriating customers with surprise cost overruns; one Redditor typically spending $100–$250/month burned $70 in a single night at launch. Reviews cite community reports of $45–$350 in a single session, projects becoming "up to 4x higher" after the shift to effort-based billing, and the recurring complaint of paying credits to build a feature then paying more when the Agent breaks it. Replit's own pricing page lists "Effort-Based Pricing (pay-as-you-go)" as a FAQ topic without defining it on the page.

weaknesses.issue: Hostinger's cheap tiers are structurally expensive: 30 prompts/month AND no code editor
weaknesses.evidence: Explorer gives 30 credits/month. Reviewers state "if you're iterating heavily on a design: 'move this left,' 'make the font bigger,' 'add a dropdown menu': you can burn through 30 prompts in a single sitting. This is the single biggest friction point." The code editor is gated at Hobbyist ($39.99), so Explorer and Starter users must spend a credit on every CSS tweak. The free plan's 5 credits are widely described as burning out immediately.

weaknesses.issue: Emergent's public reputation is poor and credits burn unpredictably
weaknesses.evidence: Trustpilot score reported around 2.7/5 with heavily split reviews. r/vibecoding users report credits "burn way too fast", the agent getting stuck mid-task, and buggy or misunderstood output. An Aug 2026 hands-on found visual defects on the generated site ("Get Started CTA overlapped the features section", misaligned icon-text pairs) and design edits failing outright — a 3D icon request reverted to 2D with drop shadows. Browser previews expire after 30 minutes and an active deployment costs 50 credits/month in ongoing rent.

weaknesses.issue: Wix Harmony is a lock-in dead end: no code export, no custom code, and incomplete parity with the classic editor
weaknesses.evidence: Wix's own documentation confirms Harmony does not support custom code and that Harmony sites cannot be exported and continued elsewhere; commentators note the only option if needs change is to rebuild from scratch on another platform. Reviewers add that feature maturity is the biggest limitation with no parity to the traditional Wix Editor, that auto-responsive design "fights you for control" on precise logo placement, and that "restarting is often easier than fixing an off-target first draft".

weaknesses.issue: Wix Harmony's generation makes semantic errors that look correct until inspected
weaknesses.evidence: A reviewer briefing it on a sustainable clothing store got a layout titled "The Art of Food" with a hero image of someone eating, because the word "organic" in the sustainability description triggered a culinary category. The same review found the AI "builds buttons, but it does not always link", with a published "Shop Now" CTA left entirely unconnected to the Shop page — a broken conversion path shipped live.

weaknesses.issue: Figma Make has no real version history, which is jarring given Figma's core product
weaknesses.evidence: Figma's answer is that there is no additional file-level version history in a Make file; versions mean builds, recovered by finding them in the AI chat and clicking "Restore this version". A standing feature request thread exists on the Figma forum asking for version history in Make.

weaknesses.issue: Hostinger's undo/restore is destructive and non-refunding, and the builder/control-panel seam is dangerous
weaknesses.evidence: Docs state Undo permanently deletes the last message and response, Restore confirms "All your messages after this message will be permanently deleted", and neither reinstates spent credits. Separately, changing a Horizons project's domain in hPanel "resets your email plan and deletes all associated email data" — the bundled stack's seams can destroy user data.

weaknesses.issue: Anything (ex-Create.xyz) has persistent reliability and persistence problems
weaknesses.evidence: Reviews report that "basic actions like adding images or editing components often break or require manual fixes" and that "For a no-code builder, that kills productivity", with reliability, project persistence and overall polish cited as recurring user concerns despite the autonomous "Max" agent's browser self-testing.

weaknesses.issue: Rocket.new's credit consumption is unforecastable by the vendor's own framing
weaknesses.evidence: Pricing analysis notes "credits are like your working balance" but "it's not always easy to predict exactly how many credits you'll use", creating unpredictable costs. The free tier is 20 one-time credits — sufficient to evaluate the workflow but not to do project work. Generated code is described as suiting CRUD apps and prototypes but often needing manual cleanup for complex business logic or production performance.

weaknesses.issue: Webflow AI produces competent but strategically empty output and paywalls publishing
weaknesses.evidence: 2026 assessments say it "still falls short when it comes to strategy, brand differentiation, conversion-focused UX, advanced CMS architecture, SEO, accessibility, and complex interactions." You can generate and edit for free but cannot publish to a custom domain without a Basic Site plan (from $14/mo annual), and AI features require a paid Workspace plan (Core $19/mo and above).

weaknesses.issue: Google abandoned Firebase Studio outright, a reminder that free platform tools carry discontinuation risk
weaknesses.evidence: Firebase Studio (formerly Project IDX) shut down 19 March 2026 with Cloud IDE and AI code generation discontinued; existing projects remain accessible only until March 2027 for migration. Anything built on it must be moved. Same vendor, same category, roughly one year of life.

pricing_2026:
HOSTINGER HORIZONS (verified on hostinger.com/horizons/pricing, Aug 2026): Free $0 — 5 AI credits, 1 website, no mailbox, no free domain, no card required. Explorer $6.99/mo promo (regular $9.99), $83.88/12mo, renews $6.99 — 30 credits/mo, 1 website, 1 mailbox per website, NO free domain, hosting + version history. Starter $13.99/mo promo (regular $19.99), $167.88/12mo — 70 credits/mo, up to 25 websites, 2 mailboxes per website, FREE DOMAIN, subscription + product sales, chatbots, analytics, voice/image prompts, collaboration. Hobbyist $39.99/mo promo (regular $55.99), $479.88/12mo — 200 credits/mo, up to 50 websites, 5 mailboxes per website, free domain, plus CODE EDITOR and project duplication. A Hustler tier is reported by reviewers at $59.99–$79.99 with 400 credits and up to 50 websites — treat as unverified. Credit rule verbatim: "AI credits are used when you create or edit websites by chatting with AI. Credit usage depends on the complexity of each generation." 7-day free trial with no payment info. Undo/restore costs no credits and refunds none.

REPLIT (verified on replit.com/pricing, Aug 2026): Starter free — free DAILY Agent credits, built-in database, slides/videos/animations, publish up to 1 project, private/password-protected deployments. Core $20/mo billed annually (20% off $25 monthly) — $25 monthly credits, 5 collaborators, 2 parallel agents, unlimited workspaces, branding badge removal. Pro $95/mo billed annually (5% off $100 monthly) — $100 monthly credits, 15 collaborators, 50 viewers, 10 parallel agents, premium support, 28-day database rollbacks. Enterprise custom. Deployments are billed ON TOP: scheduled and autoscale from $1/mo, reserved VM from $20/mo. Only Agent usage is stated to consume credits. "Effort-Based Pricing (pay-as-you-go)" appears as a FAQ topic with no definition on the pricing page. Domains are sold in-app across .com/.ai — per-TLD pricing NOT verified.

FIGMA (Make AI credits): Full seat monthly allowances 3,000 Professional (≈50–70 Make prompts), 3,500 Organization, 4,250 Enterprise. Starter plan and View seats 500/month plus a 150/day cap. No rollover. Full-seat limits ENFORCED from 18 March 2026. Shared team AI-credit subscription purchasable from 11 March 2026; pay-as-you-go with spend limit from Q2 2026. Reported top package ~15,000 credits for ~$350 (medium confidence, forum-sourced). Make publishing/hosting included in existing plans during beta; custom domains free through 2025 per help centre, current charging status UNVERIFIED. Custom domain caps: Professional 10, Org/Enterprise unlimited, shared between Make and Sites.

FRAMER: Free — 500 credits to try (reported elsewhere as 500/day resetting daily), 1GB bandwidth, Framer subdomain with SSL, permanent "Made in Framer" badge. Basic $10/mo — 1,000 credits/mo, 50GB bandwidth, 2 CMS collections, free custom domain. Pro $30/mo — 3,000 credits/mo, 100GB, 10 CMS collections (40 with add-ons). Scale annual-only, Enterprise custom. Reported per-action costs: landing page ~300 credits, responsive layout 150, large edit 100, small edit 50; model multipliers Sonnet 4.6 0.9x, Opus 4.8 1.8x; external agents consume no Framer credits. Free custom-domain promotion applies on yearly upgrades only.

WIX: Light $17/mo, Core $29/mo, Business $39/mo, Business Elite $159/mo on ANNUAL billing; monthly $24/$36/$46/$172. All paid plans include a free custom domain for year one, ~$17.35/yr thereafter. Custom domain support begins at Light. Free plan gets a Wix-branded domain. Harmony-specific pricing was NOT separately verified — it appears to sit inside standard Wix plans.

EMERGENT: Free $0 — 10 credits/mo. Standard $20/mo monthly, $17/mo annual (save $36) — 100 credits/mo, private hosting, GitHub, fork tasks. Pro $200/mo monthly, $167/mo annual (save $396) — 750 credits/mo, 1M context, ultra thinking, system-prompt editing, custom agents. Team $300/mo — 1,250 shared credits. Business/Enterprise custom. Top-ups $10 for 50 credits, never expire. An ACTIVE DEPLOYMENT costs 50 credits per month on an ongoing basis. Domains resold via IONOS, free first year then IONOS renewal rates.

ROCKET.NEW: Free $0 — 20 ONE-TIME credits. Build $25/mo — 100 credits/mo (a separate source says Pro $25/mo with 100 credits plus private projects and custom domains; treat naming as unsettled). Solve+Build $250/mo — 1,000 credits. Build+Intelligence $125/mo — 600 credits. Solve+Build+Intelligence $350/mo — 1,500 credits. Intelligence $100/mo — 500 credits. A Business tier at $50/mo with SSO and team features is reported elsewhere — the two sources conflict, so plan naming and the $50 tier are UNVERIFIED. Credits reportedly never expire and roll forward.

TEMPO: Free $0 — 30 credits. Pro $30/mo — 150 credits. Agent+ $4,500/mo with human-assisted development. Medium confidence, single aggregator source.

SOFTR: Free $0 — 10 app users, unlimited published apps. Basic ~$49/mo annual, $59/mo monthly — 20 users. Professional ~$139/mo annual, $167/mo monthly — 100 users. Business ~$269/mo annual, $323/mo monthly — 500 users. Enterprise custom. Annual saves roughly two months. AI Co-Builder is free to try. Medium confidence — softr.io/pricing could not be parsed directly.

WEBFLOW: AI Assistant, AI Site Builder, AI Code Components and Prompt-to-Production require a paid Workspace plan, Core $19/mo and above. Generating and editing is free; publishing to a custom domain requires a Basic Site plan from $14/mo billed annually. 2026 moved AI generation to a credit system for heavy users — credit amounts UNVERIFIED.

GOOGLE AI STUDIO: Free. Build, publish and the shareable link cost nothing. Free custom subdomain at name.ai.studio (from 10 July 2026), first-come first-served. New users get their first two Cloud Run deploys at no cost with no credit card; existing users fall under the Cloud Run free tier, with Cloud Run pricing applying beyond it. Free tier limit cited as 60 requests/minute. Firebase Studio, its predecessor, shut down 19 March 2026.

CLAUDE ARTIFACTS: Available on all plans (Free, Pro, Max, Team, Enterprise). Viewers of a shared AI-powered artifact authenticate with their own Claude account and their usage bills to THEIR subscription — the creator pays nothing for viewer usage and there is no hosting cost. Source is dated July 2025; later capability claims (20MB persistent storage, MCP, live artifacts) come from secondary 2026 coverage and are less firm.

CHATGPT: Canvas was sunset — flagged in OpenAI release notes 28 May 2026 and folded back into the standard chat interface after about eighteen months. ChatGPT Sites (describe an app, OpenAI hosts it) is available to Plus, Pro and Team subscribers. Specific Sites pricing, limits and quotas: UNVERIFIED.
